insights.insight: Ad tech charges $5–$150 CPA on probabilistic attribution; this protocol settles verified purchase confirmation at ~$0.10 per receipt — a 50–200x cost difference rooted in structural elimination of the attribution problem, not marginal optimization of it.

With Chrome deprecation joining Safari and Firefox, the cross-site tracking primitive is gone — and device fingerprinting, first-party data, and data brokers each fail on at least one of: accuracy, cross-ecosystem reach, or regulatory durability. Verified receipt signals exist outside all three failure modes.

Fetch and Ibotta hold verified receipt data but it is identity-attached and closed to third-party query; this protocol is the only system currently producing cryptographically verified, identity-free purchase signals that are externally queryable — a combination that does not otherwise exist in the market.

insights.topic: Geographic diffusion as organic demand signal
insights.insight: 25 metros reached with 10 new CBSAs entering in a single cycle — including simultaneous non-metro California, Arkansas, and Indiana — following burst-silence-burst propagation consistent with social graph spread, not paid acquisition; this pattern indicates real utility pull, not manufactured distribution.

insights.topic: Velocity recovery correlated with geographic expansion
insights.insight: Receipt velocity recovered to 0.787x this cycle after multiple cycles compressed below 0.75x, coinciding directly with the geographic burst; acceleration is at its highest recent reading (1.054x), suggesting new-market entry is driving volume, not just spreading thin.

insights.topic: Unknown merchant classification as data quality floor
insights.insight: 11% of receipts remain unresolved by merchant category, carrying a $290 average basket versus $52 for grocery — likely high-ticket or B2B transactions; any category-level targeting built on this dataset should treat that 11% as a known blind spot, not noise.
